title: Man dies in a Regina hospital after being arrested by police
subtitle: The Regina Police Service is investigating after a 37-year-old man died in hospital Thursday morning not long after being taken into custody by police.
article: Regina police say there was no physical altercation between officers and a seemingly intoxicated 37-year-old man who died Thursday shortly after his condition deteriorated and medical help was sought during his arrest.

"From the accounts of the officers, there was no use of force applied," Chief Troy Hagen told a news conference later in the day. "The arrest took place in a very orderly fashion," he said, explaining that the Regina man complied with a command to "prone out" on the lawn and was handcuffed.

"The officers approached the individual, and he was completely compliant, so the only physical aspect of the arrest was the actual handcuffing," he added. Once handcuffed, the man, whose name wasn't released Thursday, was placed on his side in a recovery position, said Hagen. When paramedics arrived, the man was moved to a stretcher and his handcuffs removed. Three officers accompanied him in the ambulance.

"Unfortunately after that, he went into cardiac arrest," said Hagen. The man was transported to the hospital, where he was pronounced dead at 6:13 a.m. - almost exactly an hour after officers first requested Emergency Medical Services and additional officers.
"No one feels good about an outcome like this. Anytime there's a loss of life, a death, it's unfortunate," said Hagen.

"We don't know how he died," he added. An autopsy is scheduled for today. In addition, police said the man appeared "intoxicated by some means," so toxicology results, which typically take some time, may also shed light on the situation.

Hagen said a total of 14 officers ended up responding by the end of the call because the first officers wanted further assistance, "not knowing potentially what situation had happened or what may happen given the environment."

However, he reiterated that there was no physical confrontation - unlike the death in October 2008 of 43-year-old Calvin Roy McLean. Two years ago, a coroner's inquest found the distraught Regina man had died of "prone restraint asphyxia," falling into medical distress after he was twice pepper strayed then held down in a prone position by five officers, some with knees on his back. That was the last time a person died in Regina during an arrest. With this fatality now classified as an in-custody sudden death, a retired Sask-atoon police officer has been appointed as an independent observer in the investigation, which also involves the Office of the Chief Coroner.
Under the Coroner's Act, an inquest must be held when a person dies in custody unless the death was from natural causes.

Police officers were initially dispatched to the 0-to-99 block of Nollet Avenue - behind the Normanview Mall - at 5:08 a.m. Thursday after two calls reporting a sick or injured person. The calls described a man partially clothed - dressed in a shirt and underwear - who was yelling and running around. Police arrived at 5:14 a.m., and radioed for an ambulance and backup officers a minute later. Paramedics were on scene in seven minutes.
Hagen said handcuffing a suspect is standard procedure during an arrest, and the man was being taken into custody because the original complaint was for someone causing a disturbance.
Medical help was sought because the man, although "compliant" as he was handcuffed without incident, was "somewhat non-responsive" to the officers' commands and questions.
"The first priority very quickly determined by the officers at the scene was to call EMS given the fact that they were concerned obviously about his overall health and well-being," said Hagen.

On Thursday morning, residents in the condominium complex where the man lived carried on with their activities. Caretakers mowed the lawn and other landscaping activities continued, while police officers entered and exited the second-floor apartment and took pictures at the scene. A small patch of lawn was cordoned off with police tape.
Some curious neighbours did venture outside to take a look at the activity taking place, but chose not to comment.

Elizabeth Popowich, police spokeswoman, said because the death technically occurred while the man was in police custody, an application was made to the Ministry of Corrections and Policing for an independent observer.
"We're still in the very early stages of that investigation and talking with anyone who had contact with him and that would include our police members, as well," she said.

Judy Orthner, a spokeswoman with the Ministry of Corrections and Policing, confirmed the appointment. "Our process moves very quickly as soon as the request is made from the police service. The independent observer is appointed just so they can get on with it," she said.
Under the Police Act, whenever there is an in-custody death, the police service that is investigating the circumstances is required to appoint an independent observer.

"It is to ensure that the police service that is doing the investigation is following proper protocols and basically to ensure that everything is done above board in that investigation," said Orthner.
Once the investigation is complete, the independent observer will submit a report to confirm that the investigation was done appropriately or suggest anything that may be done differently.
